overview: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners is the world's largest independent Coca-Cola bottler by revenue, formed by the 2016 merger of Coca-Cola Enterprises, Coca-Cola Iberian Partners and Coca-Cola Erfrischungsgetränke, and expanded in 2021 via the acquisition of Coca-Cola Amatil (Australia, New Zealand, Pacific Islands, Indonesia, Papua New Guinea) and in 2024 via the acquisition of Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines. CCEP manufactures, distributes and markets Coca-Cola trademark and other licensed non-alcoholic ready-to-drink (NARTD) beverages across 31 countries in Western Europe, Iberia, and the Australia/Pacific/Southeast Asia (APS) region. The company is UK-domiciled (Uxbridge), reports in EUR, files 20-F/6-K with the SEC as a foreign private issuer, and is dual-listed on NASDAQ (CCEP) and Euronext Amsterdam.

business_model.summary: CCEP operates a franchise bottling model: it purchases concentrates, beverage bases and syrups from The Coca-Cola Company (TCCC) and its own manufacturing subsidiaries under long-term territorial bottling agreements, then manufactures, packages, merchandises, sells and distributes finished branded beverages to retail, away-from-home (foodservice/on-premise) and wholesale customers. Revenue is transactional (paid per case/unit sold) rather than subscription-based, but is highly repeatable given daily consumption patterns, extensive retail distribution and long-standing customer relationships. Growth is driven by a mix of volume (unit cases), price/mix (headline pricing, premiumization, pack/channel mix) and FX.

revenue_streams.name: APS - Australia, Pacific & Southeast Asia (Australia, NZ, Indonesia, Philippines, PNG, Pacific Islands)

business_model.customer_type: B2B distribution to retail (grocery/convenience), away-from-home/foodservice (restaurants, QSR, hospitality), and wholesale, ultimately serving mass-market B2C consumers
business_model.geographic_mix: Europe ~74% of H1 2026 revenue (Great Britain, Iberia/Spain-Portugal-Andorra, Germany, FBN i.e. France/Monaco/Belgium/Luxembourg/Netherlands/Norway/Sweden/Iceland); APS ~26% (Australia/Pacific/PNG and Southeast Asia - Indonesia and Philippines, the latter added via the 2024 CCBPI/CCEAP acquisition)

main_competitors: Coca-Cola HBC (fellow Coca-Cola bottler, competes for investor capital and in some adjacent geographies)
Private label / retailer own-brand soft drinks
Local/regional beverage companies (e.g., in Indonesia and Philippines) and craft/independent energy and water brands
Suntory (in APS, following CCEP's exit from Suntory alcohol distribution)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest independent Coca-Cola bottler globally by revenue; #1 or #2 position in most of its territories in take-home and away-from-home NARTD channels; management cites CCEP as the #1 'value creator' for retail customers in its markets

moat_factors.description: Long-term (effectively perpetual, renewable) exclusive agreements with The Coca-Cola Company grant CCEP the sole right to manufacture, sell and distribute TCCC trademark beverages in its territories, creating a structural, regulator-sanctioned barrier to entry
Access to the Coca-Cola, Sprite, Fanta, Powerade, Monster (distribution) and other globally recognized brands underpins consumer pull that an independent bottler could not replicate alone

Extensive direct-store-delivery networks, cooler placements (>80k added in H1 2026 alone) and retail relationships across Europe and APS create logistics and shelf-space advantages difficult for smaller players to match
Large bottling/manufacturing footprint enables procurement leverage and efficiency programs, though input costs (aluminum, PET, sugar) are largely market-driven
Category management, promotional partnerships and cooler/equipment placements create some retailer stickiness, though large retailers retain bargaining power

weaknesses: Structural dependence on The Coca-Cola Company for concentrate supply, brand licensing and pricing terms; TCCC also holds a significant equity stake and board influence
Outsized exposure to sparkling/carbonated soft drinks versus faster-growing categories, and limited presence in higher-growth emerging markets compared to peers like Coca-Cola HBC
Thin bottler operating margins relative to consumer-brand owners, with profitability sensitive to input cost inflation (concentrate, aluminum, PET, sugar) and ability to pass through pricing
Geographic concentration in mature, low-growth Western European markets subject to soft consumer spending and higher soft-drink/sugar taxation
Loss of the Suntory alcohol distribution agreement in Australia/NZ removes a revenue and volume contributor in APS

growth_drivers: Zero-sugar and low/no-sugar reformulation and innovation (H1 2026 zero-sugar volumes +10%), addressing health-conscious consumer shift and regulatory sugar-tax pressure
Energy category expansion via Monster distribution and own-brand energy innovation (Ultra White, Viking Berry, Ultra Blue Hawaiian) — H1 2026 energy volumes +19%, share +230bps
Sports/hydration growth (Powerade innovation and expanded distribution, including new Indonesia launch) — H1 2026 sports volumes +12%

Southeast Asia growth engine: continued integration and margin build-out of the Philippines (CCBPI/CCEAP, acquired 2024, EBIT margin approaching ~10% target) and recovering Indonesia sparkling volumes, supported by a new route-to-market model
New Philippines manufacturing facility on track for 2027 start of production, adding capacity for Southeast Asia growth
Cooler and distribution expansion (>80k new coolers added in H1 2026, ~5% increase) and new customer wins (Parkdean Resorts, Papa John's, Domino's Australia, Marriott)
Revenue growth management: pricing, promotional optimization and premium/large-pack mix shift
Efficiency and productivity programs reducing opex as a percentage of revenue, including a shared-service center scale-up in Manila (>250 colleagues)
Technology/AI investment (SAP S/4HANA deployment, agentic AI tool 'KIRA', enhanced pricing/promo tools) to support Revenue and Margin Growth Management
Ongoing capital returns: ~50% dividend payout ratio target plus an active share buyback program (up to €1 billion, running through February 2027)

business.risk: Concentration risk with The Coca-Cola Company
business.description: CCEP's entire product portfolio and cost base depend on TCCC-set concentrate pricing, brand licensing terms and marketing support; any deterioration in this relationship would be existential

business.risk: Category and portfolio concentration in sparkling/carbonated drinks
business.description: Outsized exposure to sparkling soft drinks versus higher-growth categories/emerging markets constrains long-term structural growth versus some peers
Large grocery and foodservice customers can pressure pricing and promotional terms, and timing/effectiveness of CCEP's response to consolidation could reduce net realized pricing
Some territories permit imports of Coca-Cola products bottled by other territories, and CCEP is restricted from blocking intra-EEA imports, creating pricing/margin leakage risk

business.risk: Loss of Suntory alcohol distribution in Australia/NZ
business.description: Exit reduces APS volume and revenue comparisons through FY2026

financial.description: Revenue and costs are earned in GBP, USD, AUD, NOK, SEK, ISK, IDR, PGK, PHP and other currencies but reported in EUR; FX-neutral vs reported results can diverge materially (e.g., H1 2026 revenue +4.4% reported vs +6.1% FXN)

Net debt funds a combination of dividends (~50% payout ratio), an active ~€1bn buyback program, and M&A/capex (Philippines facility, supply chain investment), requiring continued free cash flow generation (FY guidance ≥€1.7bn comparable FCF)
Concentrate costs, aluminum, PET resin, sugar and manufacturing inflation pressured cost of sales per unit case in FY2025 and H1 2026, requiring pricing/productivity offsets

regulatory.description: Existing and potential new sugar taxes (e.g., France's 2025 sugar tax, UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy) directly affect volumes, product reformulation costs and revenue/unit-case comparisons; management explicitly flags sugar taxes as a principal risk

regulatory.risk: Packaging/environmental regulation (EPR, deposit return schemes, plastics rules)
regulatory.description: New deposit return schemes (e.g., Portugal launch in H1 2026) and extended producer responsibility rules across EU/UK/Australia raise packaging compliance costs
Structural exclusivity arrangements could attract regulatory scrutiny in some jurisdictions, though currently well-established

macro.description: Value-conscious consumer behavior in markets like Germany has weighed on volumes, with declines partly offset by mix/pricing

macro.risk: Emerging market currency and macro volatility
macro.description: Indonesia, Philippines, and Pacific Island economies carry higher currency and political/economic volatility than core European markets
Volume performance is materially affected by seasonal weather (e.g., favorable June 2026 weather and FIFA World Cup activation boosted GB/Europe volumes)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: The global non-alcoholic ready-to-drink (NARTD) beverage category is mature in developed markets (low single-digit value growth, ~3% volume growth per management-cited Nielsen/IRI data) but has structurally higher growth in Southeast Asia and other emerging APS markets; category trends favor zero/low-sugar, energy, sports/hydration and premium formats over traditional full-sugar carbonates
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate — NARTD beverages are a resilient consumer staple with high repeat purchase, though away-from-home/foodservice channel volumes and premium/large-pack mix show some sensitivity to consumer discretionary spending and weather
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — the business carries meaningful net debt to fund capex, M&A and shareholder returns; higher rates raise financing costs and can pressure capital allocation trade-offs between buybacks/dividends and deleveraging
key_input_costs: Sugar/soft-drink taxes (effectively a variable input cost)

recent_developments.event: Q2/H1 2026 results: reported revenue +4.4% (FXN +6.1%) to €10.7bn; comparable operating profit +8.1% FXN; comparable diluted EPS +10.6%; FY2026 guidance reaffirmed (revenue +3-4%, operating profit ~+7%, comparable FCF ≥€1.7bn)

UBS downgraded CCEP from Buy to Neutral (price target cut to $107 from $109); Wells Fargo raised its price target to $120 from $115 with an Overweight rating, reflecting a split analyst view on valuation
Q1 2026 trading update showed strong growth, innovation-led share gains, and reaffirmed FY2026 guidance and shareholder return plans

FY2025 results announced alongside a new up-to-€1 billion share buyback program (commenced 18 Feb 2026, expected to run through February 2027) and roughly €1 billion committed to expanding manufacturing capacity, supply chain upgrades, digital innovation and sustainability

Continued integration of Coca-Cola Beverages Philippines (renamed Coca-Cola Europacific Aboitiz Philippines, CCEAP) acquired February 2024 for $1.8bn (CCEP 60% / Aboitiz Equity Ventures 40%); Philippines EBIT margin approaching the ~10% target, with a new greenfield production facility on track for 2027
France implemented a new sugar tax, pressuring Coca-Cola Original Taste volumes in the FBN region while accelerating the shift to Coca-Cola Zero Sugar
Exited Suntory alcohol distribution agreement in Australia and New Zealand, creating a reported-volume/revenue headwind in APS that masks underlying non-alcohol business growth (~10% in H1)
Major FIFA World Cup marketing activation (500k+ displays) drove volume and share gains, particularly in Great Britain and Europe

items.notes: Reaffirmed at Q1, Q2 and H1 2026 trading updates; group guidance implies roughly Europe +2-3% within the total
Comparable basis; supported by productivity/efficiency programs and positive mix
H1 2026 interim dividend of €0.82/share (~40% of FY2025 total dividend), declared at Q1 and paid in Q2
Announced with FY2025 results, commenced 18 Feb 2026

items.metric: Cost of sales per unit case
items.notes: H1 2026 cost of sales/UC +0.6% vs +3.6% in H1 2025, reflecting easing input cost pressure though still tracking concentrate cost and tax impacts

guidance.management_commentary: Management (CEO Damian Gammell, CFO Ed Walker) characterized H1 2026 as strong, broad-based growth led by energy, zero-sugar and sports/hydration categories, with the core non-alcohol business growing approximately 10% once the Suntory alcohol exit is excluded. Management emphasized continued investment in cooler placements, customer wins, Southeast Asia scale-up (Philippines nearing target margins, new Manila facility for 2027), and technology/AI initiatives (S/4HANA, KIRA) as levers for further margin expansion, while reaffirming full-year revenue, operating profit and free cash flow guidance.

bull_case: Exclusive, effectively perpetual territorial bottling agreements with The Coca-Cola Company create a durable structural moat that is very difficult for a competitor to replicate
Diversified, resilient NARTD franchise with strong momentum in higher-growth categories (zero-sugar +10%, energy +19%, sports +12% in H1 2026) offsetting maturity in core sparkling carbonates
Southeast Asia (Philippines, Indonesia) provides a genuine long-term volume growth engine as margins converge toward group targets and new capacity comes online in 2027

Disciplined capital returns — ~50% dividend payout ratio plus an active up-to-€1bn buyback — combined with consistent free cash flow generation (≥€1.7bn FY2026 guide) support total shareholder return even if organic growth is moderate

Efficiency, technology and AI-driven productivity programs (S/4HANA, KIRA, revenue growth management tools) are expanding operating margins even as input costs and consumer value-seeking pressure gross margins
bear_case: Structural dependence on The Coca-Cola Company for concentrate supply and brand licensing limits CCEP's strategic independence and caps its share of category economics versus the brand owner

Outsized exposure to mature Western European markets and the sparkling/carbonated category constrains structural growth relative to peers with more emerging-market and total-beverage exposure (e.g., Coca-Cola HBC)
Sugar taxes and packaging/EPR regulation are an escalating, largely uncontrollable cost and volume headwind across multiple core European and Australian markets

Premium valuation versus bottling peers (e.g., Coca-Cola HBC) leaves limited room for multiple expansion and makes the stock sensitive to any growth or margin disappointment — reflected in a recent UBS downgrade to Neutral

Multi-currency reporting (GBP, USD, AUD, NOK, SEK, IDR, PGK, PHP into EUR) creates a persistent gap between strong FX-neutral performance and weaker as-reported results that can unsettle investors in periods of currency volatility
